messages.author: b6fd2925353976cd
messages.subject: fat hairy caterpillar question
parts:
Hi all,

I am fitting a hierarchical model in which one variance component sigma_w probably has a small value. I tried using a truncated (i.e., sigma_w is constrained to be greater than 0) Cauchy(0,2.5) prior and also a truncated Normal(0,1) prior. Convergence diagnostics looks fine (R-hats are 1) and I don't get any divergent transitions. I do get a message I haven't seen before in Stan.

When I look at the chains, I see indications that the mixing is not really happening for this sigma_w parameter (but R-hat is 1). In the other parameters' chains I see the usual reassuring fat hairy caterpillars. Does this figure count as indicating that something is wrong with the model specification?

thanks,

Shravan

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: fat hairy caterpillar question
parts:
Hi Shravan, 

The trace plot doesn't look horrible but there are definitely a few spots where it looks like the mixing is poor. The BFMI warning is related to the relatively new NUTS energy diagnostic that Michael introduced. How do the energy diagnostic plots look? If you haven't made those before, you can do it easily with the bayesplot package. Something like this should work:

library("bayesplot")
np <- nuts_params(stanfit)
mcmc_nuts_energy(np, merge_chains = FALSE)

Jonah

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fat hairy caterpillar question
parts:
Low E-BFMI typically means heavy tails — which you can see
in the trace plot.  The parameter shown was positive, which means
that Stan is really fitting the log of that parameter, and when you
log those traces you’ll see that those sojourns to very small values
turn into very long sojourns to explore a posterior distribution with
a heavy tail towards negative log parameter values.  This is common,
for example, in hierarchical models.

I’m really surprised that you don’t see divergences, but maybe you’re
getting more of a spike and slab geometry where the sampler takes
a long time to transition from the slab into the spike and once in the
spike it takes a long time to explore close to zero and back.

messages.author: 2ffa956ce2411d70
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] fat hairy caterpillar question
parts:
Hi there,

I just had the same problem, one of my variability parameters in a hierarchical model got stuck at 0 and looked like Shravan's plot (actually even somewhat worse). So I hope I can add something meaningful.

When following Jonah's advice of plotting the energy diagnostic the pattern was clearly pathological. What pathological means can be checked here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.00695.pdf
Fig. 3 shows a non-pathological plot (left panel) and a pathological one (right panel). Mine was clearly worse than any of those. The recommendation this paper by Michael Betancourt has is the old one: 

Within existing tools like Stan, however, perhaps the best way to deal with any identified pathologies is with alternative implementations, such as the non-centered parameterization utilized in the eight schools example.

When I followed this recommendation and moved my parameterization to a non-centered one, the problem completely disappeared. I modeled mine exactly after the eight school example given in the paper which I summarize again here. Note that I removed all model parts not relevant to the parametrization question.

More specifically, consider the original mode:

data {
int<lower=0> J;
}
parameter{
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real theta[J];
}
model {
  theta ~ normal(mu, tau);
}

Change this to:

data {
  int<lower=0> J;
}
parameters {
 real mu;
 real<lower=0> tau;
 real theta_tilde[J];
}
transformed parameters {
 real theta[J];
 for (j in 1:J)
 theta[j] = mu + tau * theta_tilde[j];
}
model {
  theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1);
}

As one can see, instead of modeling theta directly, we model theta_tilde and then set theta equal to the mean parameter plus the former variability parameter (i.e., the sigma_w in Shravan's example) times theta_tilde. This should removes the problems with tau (or sigma_w).

Hope that helps,
Henrik
